result:
Neither. The premise isn't true: more agents don't always give better results, and for your assistant the right number is probably one.

**Summary:** A multi-agent system splits a job across several model-driven loops, and each loop has its own context (the text the model can see) and its own bill. The extra agents only pay off in certain situations.

- **Why it's tempting:** More specialists sounds like a deeper bench.
- **Cost:** Every agent re-reads its own instructions and context, and every hand-off between agents adds more text. Your sponsor budget is small, so tokens (the units models are billed in) matter a lot.
- **Errors:** Each hand-off is a place for information to get lost or garbled. Ten agents means many more of those places than one agent has.
- **When splitting pays off:**
  - the work is big enough that one context overflows
  - subtasks are independent and can run in parallel
  - the subtasks need very different tools or instructions
- **Your assistant:** It answers from manuals, checks a calendar and books time. That is three tools in one short loop, so it fits comfortably in a single agent. Parts of it could be fixed workflow steps instead.

**Sports analogy:** A soccer team with 22 players on the pitch isn't better. It's just chaos. Add a player only when a position needs covering.

**Quick question:** For a request like "Book the laser cutter Thursday and tell me the safety rules", would a second agent be doing work the first couldn't?

If you want the full decision rule, I can write a lesson on multi-agent systems. It's on your mission list.
